paragraphs: Optimization algorithms often rely on gradients to decide how to improve a solution, but those gradients may be inaccurate. This paper studies errors that are biased and measured relative to the gradient itself. Such errors arise when gradients are compressed, represented with reduced numerical precision, or estimated using finite differences. The central question is how these inaccuracies affect established methods for constrained optimization.

The authors analyze projected gradient and conditional gradient methods across several settings. These include optimization within a box, where each variable has bounds and gradient errors are specified coordinate by coordinate, and optimization over a general compact convex set. Their guarantees explicitly account for the size of the relative error, connecting the quality of gradient information to algorithmic convergence.

Two results stand out within the settings studied. Conditional gradient is invariant to relative error in the box-constrained, coordinate-wise error setting, while projected gradient retains convergence guarantees for nonconvex objectives. These findings identify circumstances in which approximate gradients remain compatible with reliable optimization, with conclusions tied to the particular constraints and error models analyzed.
icml-2024-a-study-of-first-order-methods.tldr: The paper establishes convergence guarantees for constrained optimization with biased relative-error gradients, including robustness results for specific methods and settings.

paragraphs: When a graph contains many nodes from some classes and few from others, learning useful node representations becomes difficult. The training loss matters because it determines which prediction errors receive attention. Carefully designed losses can use class counts and the graph's connections to address imbalance, but creating them requires expert judgment and may produce choices poorly suited to another task.

This paper proposes a framework that searches for loss functions automatically. It moves the task-specific design work into a search process, aiming to make loss selection more adaptable across graph neural networks and datasets. The contribution centers on choosing how a model learns from imbalanced graph data, where both category frequencies and relationships between nodes are relevant.

Across 15 combinations of graph neural networks and datasets, the authors report significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art methods. They also observe that homophily, the tendency of connected nodes to share similar characteristics, contributes substantially to transferability. This finding connects the usefulness of a searched loss across tasks to the structure of the graphs involved.
icml-2024-automated-loss-function-search.tldr: Automated loss-function search improves class-imbalanced node classification, with graph homophily contributing to transferability.

paragraphs: Evaluating language-model safety involves more than checking whether an adversarial prompt succeeds. Attacks can differ in fluency, tone, visibility, and how naturally they fit surrounding text. This paper studies controllable jailbreak generation: searching for attacks while also specifying attributes they should satisfy. That framing expands the range of behaviors a safety assessment can examine.

The authors connect this problem to controllable text generation and adapt an existing algorithm called Energy-based Constrained Decoding with Langevin Dynamics. Their framework, COLD-Attack, combines adversarial search with requirements involving fluency, stealthiness, sentiment, and coherence with text on either side. It supports several evaluation settings, including constrained suffixes, adversarial paraphrases, and attacks placed at specified positions in a larger context.

Experiments across six named model families report broad applicability, strong control over requested attributes, high attack success, and transferability between models. These results suggest that evaluating only one prompt format can overlook other relevant attack settings. The contribution is a unified framework for studying those variations and assessing safety under more diverse contextual requirements.
icml-2024-cold-attack-jailbreaking-llms-.tldr: COLD-Attack frames jailbreak generation as controlled text generation, enabling safety evaluations across varied linguistic and contextual constraints.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model can involve removing parts of its computation through sparsification or reducing numerical precision through quantization. Applying either approach alone can substantially degrade performance at high compression ratios. This paper introduces Joint Sparsification and Quantization, or JSQ, to coordinate the two processes and address interactions that make aggressive compression difficult.

A key interaction involves outliers: unusually large values that sparsification tends to preserve but that complicate quantization. The authors introduce a sparsity metric designed to bridge the two compression methods. They also develop a search-based activation editor that removes relatively unhelpful outliers. This distinction matters because the paper identifies outliers as both influential in model behavior and troublesome for compression.

Experiments across multiple datasets and architectures support the framework's effectiveness. For LLaMA, the authors report a 7.96-fold reduction in computation without the model crashing, contrasting this with failures of most state-of-the-art compression methods at such extreme ratios. The finding supports coordinating compression decisions around their shared obstacles; it does not establish an equivalent measured reduction in execution time.
icml-2024-compressing-large-language-mod.tldr: JSQ coordinates sparsification, quantization, and outlier editing, achieving a reported 7.96-fold computation reduction for LLaMA without crashing.

paragraphs: Black-box fine-tuning lets users adapt a language model through an interface without direct access to its internals. That flexibility also creates a safety challenge: training supplied by a malicious user may alter the model's behavior in ways that ordinary checks miss. This paper investigates whether apparently harmless training examples can collectively produce harmful behavior.

The authors introduce covert malicious fine-tuning, in which individual examples appear innocuous while the dataset teaches an association between encoded harmful requests and encoded harmful responses. The important distinction is between what an isolated example appears to contain and what the model learns across the dataset. This makes the work relevant to defenses that inspect training data or evaluate the adapted model.

Applied to GPT-4, the method produces a fine-tuned model that follows harmful instructions 99% of the time in the reported evaluation. It also evades the tested dataset inspection, safety evaluation, and input/output classification defenses. These findings challenge the adequacy of those defenses against sophisticated adaptation attacks, while raising rather than conclusively resolving the broader question of whether black-box fine-tuning can be secured.
icml-2024-covert-malicious-finetuning-ch.tldr: Apparently innocuous fine-tuning examples can collectively undermine model safety and evade the defenses tested in the paper.

paragraphs: A diffusion model can generate samples from a learned distribution, but reconstruction tasks ask a more specific question: which samples are plausible given a particular measurement? This is posterior sampling. It underlies applications such as filling missing image regions, increasing image resolution, and reconstructing MRI data. Fast ordinary sampling does not automatically establish that this measurement-conditioned task is also fast.

The paper proves a computational barrier under the cryptographic assumption that one-way functions exist. Under that assumption, there are problem instances where every posterior-sampling algorithm requires superpolynomial time, even though unconditional sampling is provably efficient. The result concerns hard instances and rules out a general efficient solution under the stated assumption; it does not say every practical reconstruction problem is difficult.

A second result uses a stronger assumption: that some one-way functions require exponential time to invert. Under this condition, exponential-time rejection sampling is essentially optimal. Together, the results explain why successful heuristic reconstruction methods need not imply a universally efficient algorithm that samples from the correct posterior distribution.
icml-2024-diffusion-posterior-sampling-i.tldr: Under cryptographic assumptions, some diffusion posterior-sampling problems are inherently hard even when unconditional sampling is efficient.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning lets an agent learn through imagined experience generated by its model of the environment. The paper asks whether this dreaming process can become more useful when it has an explicit planning structure. Its inspiration comes from observations that people organize spatial planning through a divide-and-conquer strategy, breaking a larger journey into more manageable parts.

The proposed agent, Dr. Strategy, learns landmarks in its internal representation of the environment. It then learns a highway policy conditioned on those landmarks. Within imagined experience, the agent first learns to reach a landmark and then concentrates on exploration or task achievement from that location. Landmarks therefore provide intermediate destinations that organize how the agent practices.

Experiments show improvements over prior pixel-based model-based reinforcement learning methods on several visually complex, partially observable navigation tasks. These are settings where the agent must act from visual input without seeing the entire relevant state. The findings support the value of structuring imagined experience around learned destinations for the navigation tasks studied.
icml-2024-dr-strategy-model-based-genera.tldr: Dr. Strategy organizes imagined experience around learned landmarks, improving performance on visually complex, partially observable navigation tasks.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps training data on clients, but those clients can differ in several ways at once. Their input features may have different distributions, their label frequencies may differ, and the relationship between inputs and labels may change. This paper focuses on the challenge of maintaining global performance when these forms of distribution shift occur together.

The authors identify learning difficulties created by simultaneous shifts and propose a principle for clustering clients to address them. They find that existing methods do not satisfy this principle. Their framework, FedRC, introduces a new objective and a bi-level optimization problem, using two linked levels of optimization to implement the proposed clustering approach.

Extensive experiments report significant gains over other state-of-the-art cluster-based federated learning methods. The findings support treating the coexistence of different shifts as a distinct design problem for client clustering. FedRC's contribution is therefore both conceptual and algorithmic: it specifies a clustering principle for this setting and provides a framework intended to follow it.
icml-2024-fedrc-tackling-diverse-distrib.tldr: FedRC uses a new clustering principle and bi-level optimization to improve federated learning when multiple distribution shifts coexist.

paragraphs: Language models can learn a task from examples included in a prompt, but performance depends strongly on which examples are chosen. This paper develops Example Gisting to learn representations useful for selecting examples for each new input. Supervised fine-tuning places an attention bottleneck between inputs and outputs, creating gist representations that support a selection metric called GistScore.

The authors explore two ways to train these representations. One fine-tunes a gist model for each dataset. The other trains one model across many datasets so that it can select examples for new tasks without additional task-specific training. This second option makes the resulting in-context learning pipeline training-free at deployment to a new task, despite the selector having been trained previously.

Evaluation spans 21 datasets, nine tasks, and eight language models. Dataset-specific models deliver reported absolute gains exceeding 20% over off-the-shelf retrievers and 5% over the best prior methods. The multi-task selector generalizes across tasks, datasets, and prompt templates, matching or outperforming prior selection methods while running three orders of magnitude faster than the strongest training-free baseline.
icml-2024-gistscore-learning-better-repr.tldr: GistScore learns compact representations for choosing informative prompt examples, improving in-context learning with both dataset-specific and reusable selectors.

paragraphs: A classifier can learn shortcuts that correlate with labels in training data but fail for particular groups. Methods that counter these shortcuts often need group labels identifying the spurious attributes. When those labels are unavailable, inferred labels can substitute, but the paper highlights a substantial gap in worst-group accuracy between inferred and true group information.

The proposed method, GIC, targets that gap by improving group inference itself. It trains a classifier for spurious attributes using two properties: those attributes correlate strongly with the target labels, and the strength of that relationship varies across datasets with different group distributions. These properties provide a basis for identifying group structure when explicit group labels are unavailable.

Experiments on multiple datasets show effective group inference and improved worst-group accuracy when GIC is combined with several downstream invariant learning methods. This supports its usefulness as a component in different robustness pipelines. Analysis of its errors also reveals a phenomenon called semantic consistency, which the authors suggest may help separate spurious attributes from target labels; that explanation remains a qualified possibility.
icml-2024-improving-group-robustness-on-.tldr: GIC improves inferred group labels and strengthens worst-group accuracy when combined with several invariant learning methods.

paragraphs: Domain knowledge can be difficult to incorporate into deep learning because the parts of a neural model do not necessarily correspond to recognizable entities in the application. Without that connection, even useful probabilistic prior information has no obvious place in the model. This paper addresses the problem within multiple instance learning, where learning involves collections of instances.

The authors show how to define a mapping between domain entities and components of a multiple instance learning model. Their framework, DeeMILIP, then offers several strategies for using that mapping to incorporate prior knowledge. They motivate and formalize these strategies probabilistically, giving the knowledge a defined relationship to the model instead of leaving its use as an informal design choice.

Experiments in an immune-based diagnostic application show that the strategies can produce generalizable models with weak signals, small datasets, and limited computation. The result supports a concrete way to make domain knowledge useful under those demanding conditions. Its practical evidence comes from that diagnostic case, where meaningful correspondences between model components and domain entities enable the proposed approach.
icml-2024-incorporating-probabilistic-do.tldr: DeeMILIP links domain entities to model components so probabilistic prior knowledge can support multiple instance learning with limited data and computation.

paragraphs: A diffusion model's latent space provides an internal representation from which images can be generated or manipulated. The paper identifies a problem with existing representations: attributes are entangled, and the mapping from latent space to image space is geometrically distorted. As a result, manipulating the representation does not provide the smooth, precise control that a better organized space could offer.

The authors introduce Isometric Diffusion, which adds a geometric regularizer to the model. This extra training constraint guides the learned latent space toward the geometry of the training data manifold. The goal is a more disentangled representation, where changes in latent space support more predictable changes in the resulting images.

The paper evaluates image interpolation, image inversion, and linear editing. These respectively examine transitions between images, recovery of a latent representation for an image, and attribute changes made through latent-space edits. The reported experiments support smoother interpolation, more accurate inversion, and more precise attribute control. The findings connect the geometry of the learned representation to practical image manipulation capabilities.
icml-2024-isometric-representation-learn.tldr: Isometric Diffusion adds geometric regularization to improve latent-space disentanglement, image interpolation, inversion, and editing.

paragraphs: Tabular prediction often depends on finding useful features in rows of structured data, especially when only a few labeled examples are available. FeatLLM assigns this feature-engineering role to a language model. Through in-context learning, the model generates rules and features that transform the input into a representation suited to a downstream prediction task.

A simple machine learning model, such as linear regression, then uses the discovered features to estimate class likelihoods. At inference time, predictions rely on that model and the engineered features, so individual samples do not require new language-model queries. The framework needs only API access to the language model and is designed to overcome prompt-size constraints.

Across tabular datasets from varied domains, the authors report high-quality generated rules and an average improvement of 10% over alternatives including TabLLM and STUNT. The findings support using a language model's capabilities during feature discovery while keeping the prediction stage simple. This division of work is central to the method's practical appeal for few-shot tabular learning.
icml-2024-large-language-models-can-auto.tldr: FeatLLM uses language models to engineer tabular features, then makes predictions with a simple model without per-sample LLM queries.

paragraphs: A Schrödinger bridge describes a stochastic process that transports probability mass between distributions and connects diffusion modeling with entropic optimal transport. Bridge matching aims to recover such a process from a transport plan. Existing matching-based approaches face a key difficulty: obtaining the appropriate entropic optimal transport plan, often through approximations or iterative procedures that accumulate training error.

The paper proposes optimal Schrödinger bridge matching, using an optimal parameterization of the diffusion process. Its theoretical result establishes recovery of the bridge in a single matching step with an arbitrary input transport plan. Within this formulation, the starting plan therefore need not already be the entropic optimal transport solution that earlier approaches seek.

The authors also show that their matching objective coincides with recently developed energy-based modeling objectives for learning these transport processes. This connection motivates LightSB-M, a practical solver that represents an adjusted Schrödinger potential with a Gaussian mixture. Experiments demonstrate the solver on several practical tasks, connecting the theoretical matching result to an implementable learning method.
icml-2024-light-and-optimal-schrodinger-.tldr: Optimal Schrödinger bridge matching theoretically recovers the bridge in one matching step from an arbitrary transport plan and motivates the LightSB-M solver.

paragraphs: Assessing a model becomes difficult when the data distribution changes over time. Historical observations provide evidence about performance, but their relevance depends on how the environment has changed. This paper studies how to use datasets from the current period and earlier periods to estimate generalization error under unknown, potentially arbitrary temporal distribution shifts.

The authors develop an adaptive rolling window approach that adjusts the historical span used for assessment. They extend the same strategy to compare two candidate models by estimating the difference between their generalization errors. This makes relative model quality a direct target of estimation and supplies a comparison procedure for choosing among alternatives.

To select from a larger collection, the method organizes pairwise comparisons into a single-elimination tournament. The paper establishes near-optimal model selection and supports the approach through theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. Together, the contributions link adaptive use of historical data to both performance estimation and model choice, with the reported results emphasizing responsiveness to non-stationary data.
icml-2024-model-assessment-and-selection.tldr: Adaptive rolling windows estimate model performance under temporal shift and support near-optimal selection through pairwise tournaments.

paragraphs: In the setting studied here, networked agents each own a classifier for the same task and revise their predictions using what other agents communicate or predict. Errors can therefore spread through social influence. A highly influential agent with an inaccurate classifier may reduce accuracy across the network, making the placement of a limited number of corrections important.

The paper asks which classifiers should have their predictions fixed to obtain the greatest network-wide benefit. It considers two objectives: an aggregate objective concerned with overall accuracy and an egalitarian objective concerned with how improvements are distributed. Distinguishing them makes explicit that maximizing total benefit and pursuing a more egalitarian outcome are separate optimization goals.

The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm for the aggregate objective and prove that optimizing the egalitarian objective is NP-hard. They also develop approximation algorithms for egalitarian improvement. Mathematical analyses provide performance guarantees, while experiments on synthetic and real data support the algorithms. The results show how the chosen social objective changes the computational difficulty of targeted corrections.
icml-2024-optimally-improving-cooperativ.tldr: The paper develops algorithms for improving networked classifiers and shows that aggregate and egalitarian objectives have different computational difficulty.

paragraphs: Motion understanding involves learning representations that can support several related tasks. ProtoFormer approaches this through prototypes: representative motion patterns that organize how a model interprets a scene. The paper combines prototype learning with a Transformer in a unified framework, with its design explicitly taking motion dynamics into account.

Two components implement the approach. Cross-Attention Prototyping discovers prototypes associated with characteristic motion patterns, providing a more transparent basis for understanding motion scenes. Latent Synchronization then uses those prototypes to guide feature learning and reduce motion uncertainty. The prototypes thus serve both as an organizing representation and as guidance for learning the features used by the model.

The reported experiments show competitive performance on optical flow and scene depth, along with applicability to object tracking and video stabilization. These results support the framework's generality across several motion-related tasks. The stated finding is that prototype-guided representations can work across this range of applications, with competitive task performance rather than a claim of uniformly surpassing every alternative.
icml-2024-prototypical-transformer-as-un.tldr: ProtoFormer uses learned motion prototypes to guide Transformer representations and achieve competitive results across several motion-related tasks.

paragraphs: A single federated model can serve some clients better than others. Fairness-aware aggregation addresses this by adapting how client contributions are combined using signals from participating clients. This paper shows that existing strategies can be understood within online convex optimization, framing the server's aggregation choices as a sequence of decisions made over training rounds.

That shared formulation lets the authors identify suboptimal design choices and propose improvements in a method called AAggFF. They develop separate versions for cross-device and cross-silo federated learning to account for the practical requirements of each setting. The central idea is to improve the server's ongoing decision process as it responds to client information.

Theoretical analysis gives sublinear regret bounds: O(sqrt(T log K)) for cross-device learning and O(K log T) for cross-silo learning, with K clients and T rounds. These bounds characterize cumulative decision quality within the optimization framework. Experiments additionally show better client-level fairness than existing methods in both settings, providing empirical support for the proposed aggregation improvements.
icml-2024-pursuing-overall-welfare-in-fe.tldr: AAggFF treats fairness-aware federated aggregation as sequential optimization, providing regret guarantees and improved empirical client-level fairness.

paragraphs: Some machine learning problems constrain matrix-valued variables to a curved space, or manifold. Riemannian optimization respects those constraints while moving toward a better objective value, but conventional updates change all variables at each iteration. This paper develops a general coordinate descent framework that updates only a few variables while preserving the required manifold structure.

The authors construct algorithms for several matrix manifolds, including Stiefel, Grassmann, hyperbolic, symplectic, and symmetric positive definite or semidefinite spaces. The significance of the framework is that selective updates remain compatible with these geometric constraints. This brings the low per-iteration cost of coordinate descent to problems where an arbitrary partial matrix update might violate feasibility.

They also introduce a more efficient variant based on a first-order approximation of the objective. Convergence and complexity analyses accompany the algorithms, and experiments illustrate their effectiveness in several applications. The work therefore combines a broad method for constructing constrained partial updates with theoretical analysis and practical evidence, emphasizing computationally inexpensive iterations across multiple geometries.
icml-2024-riemannian-coordinate-descent-.tldr: The paper develops coordinate descent methods that make inexpensive partial updates while preserving matrix-manifold constraints.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction turns a model's output into a set of possible labels, targeting a user-chosen probability that the true label is included. The paper examines how this protection can be undermined by manipulated data. It considers both evasion, where an adversary changes a test example, and poisoning, where the calibration data used to construct prediction sets are perturbed.

The authors derive robust sets by bounding how much conformity scores can change in the worst case. Those scores determine how candidate labels are judged when building a prediction set. Accounting for their possible movement provides a route to mathematical robustness guarantees. Tighter bounds also produce more efficient sets, reducing the conservatism needed to accommodate the considered perturbations.

The framework covers continuous data and discrete sparse data. Its guarantees address evasion and poisoning, including changes to features and labels. The contribution connects robustness with the usefulness of the resulting prediction sets: controlling score uncertainty more precisely allows the method to retain protection while avoiding unnecessarily broad sets under the analyzed attacks.
icml-2024-robust-yet-efficient-conformal.tldr: Tighter worst-case bounds on conformity scores yield provably robust and more efficient prediction sets under evasion and poisoning attacks.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting becomes difficult when the statistics of a series change between historical training data and future observations. Normalization tries to remove some of that statistical drift before prediction, then restore the relevant statistics afterward. This paper asks which statistics should be removed and restored, arguing that heuristic choices may overlook characteristics of the particular series.

The authors propose that useful normalization statistics should be locally invariant while varying globally. This connects stability over a local window with the need to account for changes across a longer history. Their method, Selective and Interpretable Normalization, or SIN, maximizes covariance between a look-back window and its subsequent future values to identify relevant statistics and learn the corresponding transformations.

The framework also offers an explanation for the successes and limitations of some existing normalization methods. When integrated into several established forecasting models, SIN improves their reported performance. These results support treating normalization as a learned, selective component of forecasting, with the selection tied to relationships between past observations and future values.
icml-2024-sin-selective-and-interpretabl.tldr: SIN learns which time-series statistics to normalize and how to transform them, improving several forecasting models.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning aims to learn a policy from a fixed dataset while satisfying constraints. Some tasks involve rules about how behavior unfolds over time, together with logical relationships between requirements. The paper argues that existing supervised approaches with conditioned policies do not adequately handle this richer structure in complex tasks.

The proposed Specification-conditioned Decision Transformer, or SDT, combines signal temporal logic with the sequence-modeling capabilities of a Decision Transformer. Temporal logic expresses the rules an agent should follow, and the policy is conditioned on those specifications. This gives the model a way to connect its sequential decisions to requirements that describe behavior across time.

On DSRL benchmarks, the authors report better learning of safe, high-reward policies than existing approaches. SDT also shows good alignment with different requested degrees of specification satisfaction. That result suggests the conditioning signal can meaningfully influence how closely behavior follows the temporal rules. The evidence is empirical and supports controllability across requested satisfaction levels within the evaluated setting.
icml-2024-temporal-logic-specification-c.tldr: SDT conditions an offline decision-making model on temporal-logic specifications, improving empirical safety, reward, and alignment with requested satisfaction levels.

paragraphs: Solving partial differential equations is essential in many scientific and engineering applications. Traditional numerical methods can have efficiency limitations for some formulations, while neural approaches often lack mathematical assurances that their solutions are correct or that their iterations converge. This paper develops UGrid, a neural solver for linear PDEs that addresses those assurance requirements.

UGrid integrates a U-Net with a multigrid method in a principled construction. The authors provide proofs of convergence and correctness for the proposed solver. They also introduce a residual-based loss that enables unsupervised training and offers greater stability and a larger solution space than the earlier losses considered. The training objective is thus part of the solver's design contribution.

The reported results show high numerical accuracy and strong generalization across input geometries, input values, and multiple PDE formulations. These findings accompany the mathematical analysis, connecting the solver's guarantees with its demonstrated behavior. The work's scope is linear PDEs, where it presents a way to combine learned computation with the rigor expected of a numerical solver.
icml-2024-ugrid-an-efficient-and-rigorou.tldr: UGrid combines U-Net and multigrid for linear PDE solving, with convergence and correctness proofs and an unsupervised residual loss.

paragraphs: A learned surrogate for a time-dependent partial differential equation should ideally handle changing equation parameters, different spatial and temporal resolutions, and predictions beyond observed times. The paper notes that prevalent architectures lack at least one desirable capability, while Transformer-based approaches also face quadratic time and memory costs. It introduces Vectorized Conditional Neural Fields, or VCNeFs, to address these challenges.

VCNeFs represent the evolving solution as a neural field queried at positions in space and time. They evaluate multiple query points in parallel and use attention to model dependencies among their solutions. The field can also be conditioned on the initial conditions and the PDE parameters, making those quantities explicit inputs to the learned solution representation.

The design targets a broad set of surrogate-model requirements, including support for one-, two-, and three-dimensional equations and efficient longer rollouts. Extensive experiments find VCNeFs competitive with, and often better than, existing machine learning surrogates. The reported findings support combining a conditional field representation with coordinated parallel queries as a useful approach to parametric, time-dependent PDE modeling.
icml-2024-vectorized-conditional-neural-.tldr: VCNeFs solve time-dependent parametric PDEs through conditional neural fields that jointly evaluate multiple space-time queries using attention.

paragraphs: Large images can contain both fine details and important relationships across distant regions. Downsampling sacrifices detail, while cropping reduces the context available to a model. This tradeoff matters in applications such as satellite imagery, where recognizing a local feature may depend on understanding its larger surroundings. The paper introduces xT to combine these two scales of information.

xT is a two-stage streaming architecture for vision Transformers. It adapts existing vision backbones and long-sequence language models to aggregate local details with global context. The design supports end-to-end modeling of large images on contemporary GPUs without quadratic memory growth, addressing a computational obstacle to retaining information over large image areas.

The authors evaluate benchmarks selected to test understanding of fine details across large scales. They report classification accuracy improvements of up to 8.6% and an F1-score increase of 11.6 for context-dependent segmentation, using images as large as 29,000 by 29,000 pixels. These results support the value of preserving both local information and broader context in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-xt-nested-tokenization-for-lar.tldr: xT combines local detail and global context in very large images through a streaming architecture without quadratic memory growth.
